title: Norharmane prevents muscle aging via activation of SKN-1/NRF2 stress response pathways

sections.abstract: Sarcopenia, the age-related decline in muscle mass and function, is a significant contributor to increased frailty and mortality in the elderly. Currently, no FDA-approved treatment exists for sarcopenia. Here, we identified norharmane (NR), a β-carboline alkaloid, as a potential therapeutic agent for mitigating muscle aging. We aimed to determine the ability of NR to delay muscle aging in Caenorhabditis elegans ( C. elegans ), mouse, and muscle cells in mice and humans. NR treatment improved swimming ability and increased the maximum velocity in aged C. elegans . Transcriptomic analysis revealed that NR upregulated detoxification genes in C. elegans , including cytochrome P450, UGT, and GST enzymes. NR-induced benefits were dependent on the SKN-1/Nrf2 stress response pathway. In mammalian models, NR delayed cellular senescence in human skeletal muscle myoblasts and enhanced myogenesis in C2C12 cells and primary aged myoblasts. NR supplementation in aged mice prevented muscle loss, improved muscle function, and reduced markers of cellular senescence. We found that the p38 MAPK pathway mediated NR activation of Nrf2 by disrupting the Nrf2-Keap1 interaction. NR also improved oxygen consumption rates and promoted mitochondrial biogenesis. These findings suggest that NR is a promising candidate for preventing sarcopenia and improving muscle health.
sections.introduction:
Oxidative stress plays a pivotal role in muscle aging, primarily through the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) which can damage mitochondria, cell membranes, DNA, proteins, and lipids [ 1 ]. Oxidation of muscle contractile proteins such as actin and myosin causes myofibrillar weakness and results in decreased force production in skeletal muscle fibers [ 2 ]. Muscle weakness occurs earlier and progresses faster than the atrophy and contributes to loss of muscle strength [ 3 ]. Moreover, loss of the antioxidant enzyme, SOD1 leads to a reduction in muscle strength, along with diminished membrane excitability, dysregulated calcium homeostasis, and impaired mitochondrial function, which are all hallmarks of aging muscle tissue [ 4 ]. These suggest that reducing oxidative stress could be a crucial intervention to delay sarcopenia.

The transcription factor nuclear factor erythroid 2 (NF-E2) p45-related factor 2 (NRF2) plays a critical role in the mediation of cellular antioxidant responses and maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis [ 5 ]. Under normal conditions, NRF2 remains dormant due to its binding to Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), which inhibits its transcriptional activation via ubiquitination and protein degradation [ 6 ]. When oxidants accumulate, KEAP1 dissociates from NRF2, allowing NRF2 to migrate to the nucleus, where it binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) and activates downstream antioxidative genes such as heme oxygenase (HO)-1 and NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase (NQO)-1. Long-lived organisms such as naked mole rats and Snell dwarf mice, as well as animals subjected to caloric restriction or rapamycin, exhibit high levels of Nrf2 expression (as reviewed in Ref. [ 7 ]). In contrast, Nrf2 knockout mice display a similar loss of redox capacity to that observed in aged mice [ 8 ]. Additionally, disruptions in Nrf2-Keap1 have been reported in the skeletal muscle of sedentary older humans. These disruptions, followed by diminished expression of Nrf2 target genes with age, are associated with increased muscle ROS production, glutathione depletion, and elevated oxidative damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids in both humans and rodents [ 8 , 9 ]. Researches on the Nrf2 homolog SKN-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans ( C. elegans ) and the Drosophila homolog CncC also suggest that Nrf2 plays a role in longevity by modulating the oxidative stress response [ 10 , 11 ]. Given these findings, it is likely that inducers of NRF2 activity will lead to the development of anti-aging or anti-disease drugs, and NRF2 may be a promising target for the regulation of age-related diseases and sarcopenia in humans.

β-Carbolines are naturally occurring plant-derived alkaloids that are derivatives of iodole (reviewed in Ref. [ 12 ]). The chemical structure of β-carbolines is related to the nonpolar heterocyclic aromatic amines. Norharmane (NR) and its derivatives harman and harmin are most frequently identified compounds of this group. Coffee is the most important food source of β-Carbolines, because these compounds are formed during roasting of coffee beans [ 13 ]. β-Carbolines are also found in many other food products such as soy sauce, wheat vinegar, cocoa, and alcoholic beverages [ 14 ]. Thus, foods containing β-carbolines are an important exogenous source of these alkaloids in humans. β-Carbolines exhibit several pharmacological activities, including antioxidant [ 15 ], neuroprotective [ 16 ], and anti-cancer properties [ 17 ]. The feeding of β-carboline-enriched chicory extract was reported to downregulate pro-apoptotic and neurogenerative disease-associated genes in aged rats [ 18 ]. Recently, it was reported that NR is produced by Lactobacillus -mediated tryptophan metabolism and plays a role as a modulator of the innate immune system and exerts anti-inflammatory activity [ 19 ]. However, the exact role of NR in regulating muscle aging has not yet been investigated.

This study aimed to elucidate the effects of NR on muscle aging and longevity in animals. Our findings demonstrate that NR prevents age-related muscle loss and age-associated mitochondrial dysfunction in C. elegans and mice, and improves the longevity of C. elegans . We validated the effect of NR on the prevention of muscle aging through analysis in human skeletal muscle cells. Our studies have also revealed the mechanism driving the anti-aging effects of NR via the stress response signals SKN-1/NRF-2 in C. elegans and mice.
sections.methods: The following nematode strains were sourced from the Caenorhabditis Genetics Center at the University of Minnesota in the United States: Bristol N2 (wild-type), TJ1060 spe-9(hc88) I; rrf-3(b26) II, CL2166 dvIs19 [(pAF15)gst-4p:GFP::NLS] III. , PD4251 ccIs4251 [(pSAK2) myo-3p:GFP::LacZ::NLS + (pSAK4) myo-3p:mitochondrial GFP + dpy-20(+)]; dyp-20(e1282), QV225 skn-1 (zj15) IV, CW152 gas-1 (fc21), TK22 mev-1 (kn1), MQ887 isp-1 (qm150), CB4876 clk-1 (e2519), as well as Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) OP50. These strains were reared at a temperature of 20 °C on nematode growth medium (NGM) supplemented with E. coli OP50.

To find novel candidates that can mitigate the decline of muscle activity with aging, we screened 300 compounds from the Screen-Well® Natural Product library (BML-2865) using C. elegans . Muscle activity was assessed at the mid-age stage (day 7 of adulthood) by counting the number of body bends in liquid conditions ( Fig. 1 A) (see details in Materials and Methods). The initial screening identified five materials compounds - sanguinarine, caryophyllene, curcumin, citrinin, and NR-that improved motility in aged worms compared to that in the control worms. Among these, sanguinarine [ 20 ], caryophyllene [ 21 ], and curcumin [ 22 ] have been previously reported to delay aging in C. elegans . Citrinin has been reported to be toxic in mammalian species [ 23 ]. However, the biological effects of NR on muscle aging are not well understood. In the first screening, NR-treated aged worms exhibited more active movement compared to control worms (Video S1). We observed that the number of body bends was significantly higher in the NR-treated worms than that in the control worms on day 9 of adulthood (7.1/10sec for Con vs. 12.5/10sec for NR, p < 0.001) ( Fig. 1 B). We then assessed physical activity by measuring maximum velocity (MV) as previously reported [ 24 ]. The average MV of NR-treated worms was two-fold higher than that of control worms (0.12 mm s −1 control for Con vs. 0.23 mm s −1 for NR, p < 0.01) ( Fig. 1 C). These results imply that NR inhibits the decline in muscle activity associated with aging in C. elegans .

Next, we examined the effects of NR on the longevity of C. elegans . We found that NR treatment extended the median lifespan (MDL) by 35.29 % compared to the control group (17 days for Con vs. 23 days for NR, p < 0.01) ( Fig. 1 D and Table S4 ). A similar increase in lifespan was observed when NR treatment began at the young adult stage ( Fig. 1 E). The MDL of NR-treated adult worms increased by 33.33 % compared to that of control adult worms (16.5 days for Con vs. 22 days for NR, p < 0.001) ( Fig. 1 E and Table S4 ). All of these results suggest that NR extends the health span in C. elegans .

To investigate the molecular mechanism of NR as an anti-aging agent, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis to compare differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between control and NR-treated worms on day 2 of adulthood ( Fig. 2 A). We analyzed the expression levels of 16,007 genes, representing most of the coding genes of C. elegans , and found that 964 genes (6.02 %) showed over 2-fold differential expressions ( p < 0.05) in NR group. This included the upregulation of 250 genes and the downregulation of 714 genes ( Fig. 2 B). Enrichment analyses using the Gene Ontology of Biological Processes (GOBP) and Cellular Compartments (GOCC) [ 25 ], revealed that genes involved in various regulatory processes, including oxidation-reduction, cellular glucuronidation, and the innate immune response, were upregulated in NR-treated worms. In contrast, genes associated with the defense response, epithelial cell development, regulation of proteolysis, cilium assembly, and neurogenesis were downregulated ( Fig. 2 C). As shown in Table S5 , many genes involved in the detoxification system (cytochrome p450 [CYP] genes: cyp-13A7 , cyp-14A1 , cyp-29A3 , cyp-29A4 , cyp-33C9 , cyp-33D1 , cyp-35A2 , cyp-35A3 , cyp-35A4 , cyp-35C1 , and cyp-35D1 ; uridine diphosphate [UDP]-glucuronosyltransferase [UGT] genes: ugt-1 , ugt-8 , ugt-13 , ugt-14 , ugt-16 , ugt-17 , ugt-21 , ugt-22 , ugt-25 , ugt-33 , ugt-36 , ugt-39 , ugt-40 , ugt-41 , ugt-46 , ugt-63 , ugt-65 , and ugt-66 ; glutathione S-transferase [GST] genes: gst-4 , gst-5 , gst-21 , and gst-35 ; P-glycoprotein [PGP] genes: pgp-1 , pgp-12 , and pgp-15 ) were upregulated in the NR-treated groups. The detoxification system consists of three steps: production of water-soluble intermediates (step 1), neutralization of toxic intermediates (step 2), and excretion of these neutralized intermediates (step 3). Specific enzymes are involved in each step of the detoxification process: CYPs and short-chain dehydrogenases/reductases (SDRs) in step 1, UGTs and GSTs in step 2, and PGPs in step 3. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis confirmed that NR treatment significantly increased the expression of genes involved in detoxification, including cyp-35A2 , cyp-35A4 , ugt-13 , ugt-22 , ugt-63 , gst-4 , gst-5 , pgp-1 , and pgp-12 ( Fig. 2 D). In C. elegans , the transcription factor SKN-1, which resembles the mammalian transcription factor Nrf2, orchestrates the response to oxidative stress [ 26 ], activates the detoxification response, promotes resistance to oxidative stress, and increases lifespan [ 27 ]. Thus, we tested whether SKN-1 mediated the effects of NR. We treated NR in skn-1 (zj15) mutant strains and found that NR failed to prevent the decline of muscle activity in aged mutant strains ( Fig. 2 E). Moreover, NR treatment did not extend the lifespan of skn-1 (zj15) mutant strains ( Fig. 2 F). These data indicate that SKN-1 is necessary for the anti-aging effects of NR in C. elegans . To elucidate the mechanism by which SKN-1 mediates the effects of NR we investigated whether NR modulates SKN-1 activity by measuring the transcriptional expression of gst-4 , a SKN-1 target gene. qRT-PCR analysis revealed that gst-4 expression was induced by NR in wild-type worms (3.1-fold, p < 0.001) compared to control worms. However, this upregulation was not observed in skn-1 (zj15) mutant stains ( p < 0.001) ( Fig. 2 G). Additionally, we examined in vivo gst-4 expression using the CL2166 and QV224 strains, which express fluorescent reporters indicating gst-4 promoter activity in wild-type and skn-1 mutant backgrounds, respectively [ 28 ]. NR treatment significantly increased gst-4 p::GFP expression in the CL2166 strain, whereas no such induction was observed in the QV224 strain due to the skn-1 mutation ( Fig. 2 H). These data collectively suggest that NR enhances muscle activity in aged worms and extends their lifespan through SKN-1 activation.

As we observed the preventive effects of NR on muscle aging in C. elegans, we examined the effect of NR on muscle cell senescence. NR showed no cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 10 μM in HsMMs ( Fig. 3 A). We administered NR to replicative senescent HsMMs and measured cellular senescence markers. When NR was administered to replicative senescent HsMMs, it significantly reduced the number of SA-β-galactosidase-positive cells in a dose-dependent manner ( p < 0.001) ( Fig. 3 B). NR also reduced the expression level of cellular senescence markers such as p16 ( p < 0.05) and p21 ( p < 0.005) ( Fig. 3 C and D). We further investigated the myogenic capacity of NR. NR enhanced the myogenesis of C2C12 myoblasts in a dose-dependent manner, as evidenced by an increase in the fusion index ( Fig. 3 E and F). NR also upregulated the expression of myogenesis-related genes, including MyoD and MyoG ( Fig. 3 G). To determine whether NR exhibits myogenic capacity in aged myoblasts, we treated primary myoblasts isolated from aged mice (21 months old) and compared them with young primary myoblasts (5 months old). As shown in Fig. 3 H and I, the diameter of primary myotubes from aged mice was significantly smaller than that from young mice (38 μm for young vs. 12 μm for aged mice, p < 0.001). However, NR treatment increased the diameter of aged myotubes (32 μm; p < 0.001). Moreover, NR upregulated the mRNA expression of myogenesis-related genes, such as MyoD and Myf5 , in aged myoblasts ( Fig. 3 J and K). These results suggest that NR enhances myogenesis in both C2C12 cells and primary myoblasts derived from aged mice muscle. Since SKN-1 mediates the effects of NR in C. elegans , we investigated whether this mechanism also applies to mouse and human muscle cells. First, we quantified the Nrf2 transcriptional activity by measuring the binding rate between active Nrf2 isolated from nuclear fraction of primary mouse myoblasts and Nrf2 consensus binding sequence. NR treatment significantly increased Nrf2 transcriptional activity in aged myoblasts compared to control aged myoblasts ( Fig. 3 L). NR treatment also significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of the detoxification gene, GSTA1 , an NRF2 target gene, in aged myoblasts ( Fig. 3 M). Western blot analysis further confirmed that NR increased the total and phosphorylated Nrf2 expressions along with its downstream target, NQO-1 and decreased Keap1 expression ( Fig. 3 N). Knockdown of Nrf2 using siRNA diminished the myogenic effect of NR ( Fig. 3 O) as well as the upregulation of Nrf2 and GSTA1 by NR ( Fig. 3 P and Q). These findings suggest that NR suppresses myoblasts senescence via Nrf2 activation.

We further analyzed the effects of NR on the prevention of muscle aging in mice. Eighteen-month-old mice were fed NR-supplemented diet for three months, and muscle function was analyzed in these aged mice (21 months old) through grip strength and running endurance tests. NR treatment resulted in a significant improvement in grip strength in aged mice ( p < 0.05) ( Fig. 4 A). Additionally, NR significantly increased running time in aged mice in a dose-dependent manner compared to untreated aged mice ( p < 0.05) ( Fig. 4 B). NR supplementation also led to an increase in lean body mass and prevented age-related muscle mass loss ( Fig. 4 C–E). Immunofluorescence staining of the laminin revealed that NR supplementation increased cross-sectional area (CSA) of the gastrocnemius muscle ( Fig. 4 F–H). During the experimental period, the survival probability of mice supplemented with NR was higher than that of non-supplemented control mice. By 75 weeks of age, the survival rate of aged mice had decreased by 75 %, whereas aged mice treated with NR maintained a 90 % survival rate ( Fig. 4 I). Furthermore, we observed decreased intensity of SA-β-galactosidase staining in the gastrocnemius muscle of NR-fed mice ( Fig. 4 J). The expression of senescence-related genes, p16 and p21, was also downregulated in the muscle tissues of NR-fed mice ( Fig. 4 K). Notably, no manifestations of tremor, a known side effect of β-carboline ingestion, were detected in NR-fed aged mice.

Additionally, NR treatment led to an increase in Nrf2 transcriptional activity in the muscles of aged mice ( Fig. 4 L), consistent with findings in primary aged myoblasts. NR treatment also activated Nrf2 signaling, as evidenced by increased levels of both total and phosphorylated Nrf2, as well as its downstream targets ( Fig. 4 M). These results suggest that NR effectively prevents muscle aging and reduces mortality in aged mice with Nrf2 activation.

Next, we investigated the underlying mechanism of NR-induced Nrf2 activation. Nrf2 is primarily regulated through its dissociation from KEAP1, which acts as a key inhibitory protein. To determine whether NR interacts with KEAP1 and disrupts its interaction with Nrf2, we performed molecular docking analysis using AutoDock4 to simulate the binding of NR to KEAP1, comparing it with the known interaction of sulforaphane with KEAP1. As shown in Fig. 5 A–B, both NR and sulforaphane were found to bind to the Kelch domain of Keap1. NR interacted with residues Ile416, Gly509, Ala510, Ala556, Leu557, Leu365, Gly365, and Arg415 of KEAP1, forming hydrogen bonds at Ala510 and Arg415 (binding affinity: 7.2 kcal/mol; Fig. 5 A). Sulforaphane, on the other hand, interacted with residues Ala510, Ile416, Val604, Val606, Ala366, Leu365, Gly462, Gly367, Arg415, Ala556, Gly509, and Leu557, forming a hydrogen bond with Arg415 (binding affinity: 4.5 kcal/mol; Fig. 5 B). The overlapping residue that interacts with both Nrf2 and these compounds is Arg415 ( Fig. 5 C). Given that the Arg415 residue in KEAP1 is crucial for the protein-protein interaction between KEAP1 and Nrf2 [ 29 ], we conducted a cycloheximide (CHX) chase assay to analyze the stability of KEAP1 protein. NR exposure increased the degradation of KEAP1, indicating that NR induces Nrf2 activation by destabilizing the KEAP1-Nrf2 binding ( Fig. 5 D). Furthermore, our investigation revealed that NR elevated Nrf2 protein levels in total and phosphorylated forms while reducing KEAP1 protein levels under oxidative stress conditions in C2C12 myoblasts ( Fig. 5 E). NR treatment also reduced the number of senescent cells and ROS production in H 2 O 2 -treated C2C12 cells ( Fig. 5 F–G). Additionally, NR prevented the reduction in muscle activity in C. elegans caused by H 2 O 2 -induced oxidative stress ( Fig. S1 ). Next, we measured the mitochondrial respiration in primary aged mouse myoblasts. Mitochondrial respiration capacity in aged myoblasts was assessed by sequential exposure to the ATP synthase inhibitor oligomycin A, FCCP, pyruvate, and electron transport chain inhibitors antimycin A or rotenone, starting from the basal condition. As shown in Fig. 6 D–E, the maximum respiration rate was 2.5-fold lower in primary myoblasts of aged mice than in those of young mice (245 pmol/min in young vs. 100 pmol/min in aged myoblasts, p < 0.001). Importantly, NR significantly increased the maximum respiration rate in aged myoblasts (125 pmol/min in aged NRH, p < 0.001). We further analyzed the effects of NR on mitochondrial function in aged mice and found that NR increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) copy number ( Fig. 6 F), citrate synthase activity ( Fig. 6 G), and ATP production ( Fig. 6 H). Additionally, NR supplementation led to a significant increase in maximum respiration rate in myofibers isolated from aged mice compared to that in the control groups ( Fig. 6 I–J), suggesting that dietary NR helps to preserve the mitochondrial function in aged mice.

Given that NR induces Nrf2 activation, we investigated whether the improvement of mitochondrial function by NR is dependent on Nrf2. NR treatment increased the maximal respiration rate in a dose-dependent manner in C2C12 myoblasts ( Fig. 6 K and L). However, this effect was abolished in Nrf2-silenced C2C12 myoblasts. ( Fig. 6 M and N). These data indicate that NR improves mitochondrial function during aging, likely through its role as an Nrf2 activator.
sections.discussion:
Our results suggest that NR represents a novel therapeutic candidate for mitigating muscle aging, as demonstrated in aged C. elegans and mouse models. We provide compelling evidence that NR significantly mitigates age-related declines in muscle activity and extends lifespan in C. elegans . Additionally, NR delays cellular senescence in HsMMs and enhances myogenic capacity in aged myoblasts. In aged mice, NR supplementation prevents muscle loss and preserves muscle function, supporting its potential anti-muscle aging effects. These benefits are mediated, at least in part, through modulation of the Nrf2-Keap1 signaling pathway. Collectively, this research underscores the potential of NR as a promising therapeutic agent for combating age-related muscle decline.

The aging process is characterized by the development of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, leading to significant damage to cellular components, including proteins, lipids, and DNA. This damage results in impaired muscle function and increased susceptibility to sarcopenia [ 33 ]. Nrf2 has been identified as a master regulator of the aging process across various species, as it is a transcription factor that controls the expression of numerous genes involved in detoxification, antioxidant defense, and mitochondrial function [ 34 ]. In the context of muscle aging, Nrf2 deficiency exacerbates age-related muscle loss and contractile dysfunction in mice [ 35 ]. Additionally, Nrf2 plays a key role in mediating the positive effects of exercise on aging muscle by promoting mitochondrial fission [ 36 ]. These findings suggest that Nrf2 is a promising therapeutic target for combating age-related sarcopenia.

In our study, NR was identified as a potent compound that improves muscle activity and extends lifespan in C. elegans . The NR-treated aged worms exhibited significant increases in motility, maximum velocity, and median lifespan compared to controls, indicating that NR effectively delays muscle aging. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that NR treatment led to substantial changes in the expression of genes associated with detoxification, particularly cytochrome P450 enzymes, UGTs, and GSTs. These enzymes play critical roles in the three-phase detoxification process, which involves converting toxic compounds into less harmful intermediates, conjugating them with more water-soluble molecules, and ultimately excreting them from the cell [ 37 ]. These gene expression changes are closely linked to the activation of Nrf2, as evidenced by the upregulation of genes involved in detoxification and mitochondrial maintenance [ 19 ]. Nrf2 activation enhances the organism's ability to neutralize and excrete harmful substances, thereby reducing the cumulative oxidative damage that is characteristic of aging tissues [ 38 ]. The upregulation of these detoxification pathways in NR-treated worms suggests that Nrf2 activation by NR enhances the cellular capacity to manage oxidative stress, thereby preserving muscle function and extending lifespan. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have highlighted the beneficial effects of Nrf2 activation in promoting cellular health and longevity [ 39 ]. The dependency of NR's effects on SKN-1, the C. elegans homolog of mammalian Nrf2, was confirmed by the lack of improvement in muscle activity or lifespan extension in skn-1 mutant stains. This finding underscores the critical role of Nrf2 in mediating the anti-aging effects of NR.

In addition to its effects in C. elegans , NR demonstrated significant benefits in mammalian muscle cells, including delaying senescence and promoting myogenesis. NR reduced markers of cellular senescence, such as SA-β-galactosidase activity and the expression of p16, and p21 in senescent HsMMs. Moreover, NR enhanced the myogenic capacity of C2C12 cells as well as primary aged myoblasts, as indicated by increased myotube formation and upregulation of myogenesis-related genes. Oxidative stress can impair myogenic differentiation by disrupting the balance of muscle-specific regulatory factors such as MyoD and myogenin, essential for muscle cell fusion and maturation [ 40 ]. Nrf2 is essential to maintain the proliferation and viability of myoblasts. In the absence of Nrf2, satellite cells show impaired differentiation, as NRF2 is responsible for modulating oxidative stress during myogenesis [ 41 ]. We found NR increases myogenesis through the transcriptional activation of Nrf2, as silencing Nrf2 abolished the myogenic capacity of NR.

Elevated Nrf2 signaling is observed in long-lived models such as naked mole rats [ 42 ], Snell dwarf mice [ 7 ], and caloric restriction [ 43 ]. Conversely, disruption of Nrf2-Keap1 signaling is observed in the muscle tissues from elderly human [ 9 ] and aged rats [ 44 ]. Aged mice show similar losses in cellular redox capacity to those observed in mice lacking Nrf2 indicating that age-related Nrf2 dysfunction may be the cause of diminished cellular redox status [ 8 ]. Activation of Nrf2 by dietary interventions such as diethylmalate or curcumin, improves muscle function in aged rodents [ 45 , 46 ]. We observed dietary supplementation of NR improves loss of muscle mass and function in aged mice. NR supplementation reduces mortality of aged mice. These findings support the idea that Nrf2 activation contributes to increased health span and longevity.

At the molecular level, our findings suggest that NR activates Nrf2 by disrupting its interaction with KEAP1, a cytoplasmic inhibitor that normally keeps Nrf2 in an inactive state [ 47 ]. Molecular docking studies indicate that NR binds to KEAP1, leading to its degradation and the subsequent release of Nrf2. Once released, Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of its target genes involved in antioxidant defense and detoxification [ 48 ]. While mammals utilize KEAP1 to regulate NRF2 activity, C. elegans lacks a direct KEAP1 homolog. Instead, worms employ WDR-23 to control SKN-1, the ortholog of mammalian NRF2 [ 49 ]. WDR-23 regulates various physiological functions by modulating SKN-1 activity [ 50 ]. In addition, WDR-23 functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, similar to KEAP1 in mammals [ 51 ]. Therefore, the regulation of SKN-1 activity by NR in C. elegans suggests that it may be controlled by an E3 ligase mechanism analogous to that in mice [ 52 ]. Additionally, we found that NR-induced Nrf2 activation involves the p38 MAPK pathway, which phosphorylates Nrf2, enhancing its stability and transcriptional activity [ 53 ]. Thus, NR induces Nrf2 activation through both KEAP1 degradation and p38 regulation, amplifying the cellular antioxidant response. This process is critical for protecting muscle cells from oxidative damage and preserving their function during aging.

Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging and is intricately linked to muscle decline, as impaired mitochondria lead to reduced energy production and increased ROS generation [ 54 ]. Our study found that NR preserves mitochondrial function by enhancing oxygen consumption rates (OCRs) and preventing mitochondrial dysfunction in aged C. elegans and mammalian muscle cells. This preservation of mitochondrial function is likely mediated by Nrf2, which regulates genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, maintenance, and stress response. In Nrf2-silenced myoblasts, the mitochondrial benefits of NR were abolished, highlighting the importance of Nrf2 in sustaining mitochondrial health and, by extension, muscle function during aging.

It was reported that essential tremor (ET) patients showed higher blood harmane concentration [ 55 ]. However, there are no relevant studies showing the contribution of exogenous or endogenous harmane for ET. We also did not observe any signs of tremor in NR-fed aged mice. Thus, NR is a safe therapeutic alternative for sarcopenia. Despite the promising results, there are limitations to our study. One notable limitation is the reliance on C. elegans and in vitro mammalian models, which may not fully recapitulate the complexity of human aging and muscle function. Additionally, while NR demonstrated significant effects in these models, the precise mechanisms through which NR impacts Nrf2 and associated pathways could benefit from further investigation. The translation of these findings to human clinical settings requires more extensive studies to assess the efficacy and safety of NR in diverse populations and its potential side effects.

Although this study primarily focuses on the mitigation of sarcopenia, it would be important to consider the broader context of the etiology of sarcopenia in the aging process. In particular, the immune system plays a key role in the aging of various organs, including skeletal muscle. Recent studies have suggested that immune aging may precede and contribute to the onset of sarcopenia [ 56 ]. The complex interplay between the aging immune system and muscle tissue involves multiple mechanisms. Chronic low-grade inflammation, often referred to as “inflammaging,” can negatively affect muscle protein synthesis and promote muscle breakdown [ 57 ]. In addition, age-related changes in T cell populations and function may impair muscle regeneration and repair processes [ 58 ]. Therefore, a more comprehensive study of these interactions, including the temporal relationship between immune system aging and the onset of sarcopenia, and potential interventions targeting immune function to mitigate muscle loss, is warranted, as such an approach could provide valuable insight into the multifaceted nature of aging and provide more holistic strategies for maintaining muscle health in older adults.

In summary, our study provides evidence that NR is a potent activator of the SKN-1/Nrf2 pathway, leading to improved muscle function, extended lifespan, enhanced detoxification, and preserved mitochondrial integrity during aging. The relevance of Nrf2 in muscle aging, as demonstrated by our findings, positions NR as a promising candidate for therapeutic interventions aimed at delaying sarcopenia and promoting healthy aging. Future research should focus on exploring the clinical potential of NR in human populations, particularly its efficacy in preventing or mitigating age-related muscle decline and associated disorders.
